content_metadata.description: A video showcasing an interview with Dan Blondal, CEO of Nano One Materials Corp, discussing their innovative technology to improve lithium battery manufacturing and reliability.

qAndA.answer: Nano One combines all the precursor steps, coating, and lithiating into one reactor, significantly reducing the number of steps and lowering costs.
qAndA.question: What is the main difference between Nano One's process for manufacturing cathode materials and conventional methods?

qAndA.answer: Their cobalt-free cathode material operates at a very high voltage, making it compatible with the requirements of solid-state batteries. It also enables fast charging, addressing a key challenge in the electric vehicle sector.
qAndA.question: Why is Nano One's technology particularly well-suited for next-generation solid-state batteries?

qAndA.answer: Nano One creates a commercially viable version of the single-crystal technology used in Tesla's research, producing a more durable cathode material that can withstand a higher number of charge cycles.
qAndA.question: How does Nano One's technology contribute to the 'million-mile battery' concept?

qAndA.answer: Nano One's process creates smaller, nanocrystalline coated material, while Tesla’s research uses much larger crystals. This makes Nano One’s process commercially viable.
qAndA.question: How does Nano One's process differ from the single-crystal technology used in Tesla's million-mile battery research?

qAndA.answer: Cobalt is expensive, has ethical sourcing concerns, and is not environmentally friendly. Eliminating cobalt reduces costs, addresses ethical concerns, and makes the manufacturing process more sustainable.
qAndA.question: Why is the elimination of cobalt from cathode materials desirable for battery manufacturers?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, I'm Ron Wartell. I'm a senior editor here with Investor Intel, and I'm talking
with Dan from Nano1 Materials. Dan is working in the lithium battery space. Their company
has new technology, new ideas on improving the manufacturer and the reliability batteries.
Can you talk more to that?
Yeah, great. I've certainly appreciate being here and being able to describe it. So we
work on the process for making the cathode materials. That's one of the electrode materials
that goes into the battery. It's comprised of lithium and nickel and manganese, or lithium
iron and phosphorus, and then a whole bunch of additives and coatings. It's a very complex,
composite material. So we have ways of improving the process for assembling all of those
atoms into the right structures, and then we have developed intellectual property and
patents for the resulting materials that come out to improve the performance, interability,
and safety of the materials.
Can you say just basically how your process is different than what the rest of us are doing?
Yeah, so in the industry right now, I'll give you a couple of different examples, but we
use different raw material supplies coming in. That helps us drive down the cost. We take
the coating and the precursor steps and the lithium steps, and we put them all into one
reactor, so we have one pot, and all goes into one, and that cuts the number of steps and
reduces the cost down. But it also allows us to form the right crystal structures very early
and spend less time in the furnace. The result is a pure crystalline material that performs
better.
So you're saying you're going to make a premium cathode material, and hopefully that'll
be wanted in the market.
Yes.
I've heard that Tesla is looking at the million-mile battery. Can you say how your process fits
into that?
Yeah, so Tesla, Tesla Researcher Jeff Don at DellHousey University did a fantastic paper
showing that you can actually push batteries out to kind of a million miles for a car.
Most of their research is based on the electrolyte. That's the liquid that goes in the battery that
connects the two electrodes.
But at the same time that they used a cathode material that was supplied from a Chinese
manufacturer, that is what we call a single crystal technology. Very large particles that
take forever to grow in a furnace, they're very expensive, and they're actually not commercially
viable.
To use that in combination with Jeff Don's and all the electrolytes to prove out this
kind of million-mile battery theory.
So happens we have intellectual property and patents that have a much smaller crystalline
nano-crystalline coated material that's very much akin to what they were using.
Chip ours is commercially viable. So we use a process that is environmentally friendly.
We have no waste stream. We combine all of the coating and the crystallization and all
of the preparation of the nickel manuines and cobalt all into one step. So it's fewer
step, there's less energy, there's less waste, and of course it results in a longer lasting
material that could lead to a more durable battery.
A more durable battery means that you can charge it faster, you can be more aggressive on
the charging, and you can be more aggressive on the range on a day by day basis.
That's really incredible. What is the next step for the company?
Where are you?
Well we've got really three different streams of technology we're working on. The one I
just described is single crystal NMC stuff. We're also doing single crystal technology
in lithium iron phosphate, which would be using electric buses or grid storage or entry
level vehicle type of applications. And interestingly enough another sort of Tesla link there, Tesla
week and a half ago, announced a deal with CATL, or at least there's a ledger deal with
CATL in China to put lithium iron phosphate in their Model 3s. And that actually speaks
right into our book because we've been saying that LFP is going to play a fun, still play
a very fundamental role in electric batteries. And Tesla's basically saying yeah we can put
this in entry level vehicles as well. We're working on the single crystal materials with
Volkswagen and a bunch of their peers in this space, although undisclosed right now we
don't have, we can't really talk about them.
Certainly, yeah.
And then we're also working on a no cobalt version of the material, which we've spoken
about extensively on investor intel in the past. And that's primarily aimed towards
next generation solid state batteries, where this material is very highly suited. It's
very high voltage. It can only be used in those kinds of batteries. And ultimately it's
got no cobalt and it's very fast charging. So we see that kind of in the five to ten
year time frame.
So those are really the three areas we're working on and we're very excited about what
the technology is going on.
That's very good. That's great innovation. Thanks for telling us that today.
Okay, great. Thank you. Appreciate being on here.

youtube_description:
"We use a process that is environmentally friendly, we have no waste stream, we combine all of the coating and crystallization and all of the preparation of nickel, manganese, and cobalt all into one step. So there are fewer steps, there’s less energy consumed, less waste, and results in a longer-lasting battery material that could lead to more durable battery." States Dan Blondal, CEO, Director & Founder of Nano One Materials Corp. (TSXV: NNO), in an interview with InvestorIntel's Ron Wortel at PDAC 2020.

Dan went on to say that Nano One has developed intellectual property and patents to make battery materials that can improve the performance, durability, and safety of batteries. Dan also spoke on Tesla’s million-mile battery. He said that Tesla has used cathode material supplied by a Chinese manufacturer in the battery. Dan said, "Nano One has intellectual property and patents that have nanocrystalline coated material which is very much akin to what they were using except ours is commercially viable." Dan also provided an update on Nano One's other battery technologies. He said that the company is working on lithium iron phosphate batteries used in electric buses, grid storage, etc. Nano One is also working on cobalt-free battery material which is aimed at next-generation solid-state batteries.
